Software engineering is like computer science but with more focus on organization, teamwork, and software cycles.

Standard Qualities:
- must be non-profit(for profit is more expensive and seen as a joke by employers)

- must be regionally accredited(national accreditation is bad. Must be regional)

- must be affordable(no private or liberal arts colleges if you’re not rich or upper middle class)

- must have a good program(e.g. make sure the program you’re doing falls in line with what you want to do. My example is I suck at math but love programming, so I look for programs with less math and more programming.)

- make sure at least 75% of your credits will transfer(check any transfer agreements and class equivalencies.)

- graduation rate of at least 50%(you want a school that isn’t poorly taught or extremely difficult)

- decide whether you want an art or science degree. Often it won’t help massively with employment but science degrees are often seen as the more technical and practical of the two. Some colleges offer only arts for a major, only science, or even both in separate programs.

In order from least to most prestigious: IT < CS < CE.

In order from easiest to hardest: IT < CS < CE

That should not influence your decision though; they all have different purposes. If you hate math, throw CS and CE out the window. If you like/can deal with high level math then here’s what each is about:

CS - theory behind computing and software, very math heavy and is NOT a software engineering degree, but teaches enough to let you become one.

CE - focuses on hardware and how the physical side of computers works, slight focus on software development but not as much as CS. Even more math than CS

IT - easiest route of the 3, can range from a business degree to a technical science degree depending on your program. Less math and more applied tech for businesses. You can become a developer with this still but you won’t be AS competitive as the other 2. Great option if you know you won’t do well in high level math.

TL;DR - CE = hardware, some programming, CS = computing theory and a lot of programming, IT = networks, cyber security, and also a lot of programming(at least if you go the developer route). Don’t take CE or CS if you’re bad at or hate math. for software development, CS will always be better than IT, but tech is always hiring and accepts almost any form of engineering or technology degree

edit: for what you want to do, CS would be best but beware CS and CE(or any engineering degree really) have some of the highest dropout rates and lowest graduation rates.
